name: The Abbasid Caliphate
title: Social Hierarchy of the Abbasid Caliphate: From Caliph to Enslaved
period: 750–945 (from the Abbasid Revolution to the Buyid takeover of Baghdad)

tiers.name: The caliph
tiers.you: You are the successor of the Prophet and commander of the faithful, named in every Friday sermon, but your viziers run the government and your Turkish soldiers may depose you.
tiers.kid: The caliph was the ruler of the Muslim empire and its leader in prayer.
tiers.rise: Only an Abbasid could be caliph, but no rule fixed the succession: caliphs named heirs among their sons and brothers, and the choice was often fought over, as in the civil war of 811–813 between al-Amin and al-Ma’mun. Most caliphs were sons of enslaved concubines.
tiers.why: The caliph was the successor of the Prophet as head of the Muslim community, its “commander of the faithful”, and the Abbasids claimed the office through descent from the Prophet’s uncle al-Abbas.

tiers.name: The Hashimite family
tiers.you: You descend from the Prophet’s clan, the noblest birth among Muslims, and may govern a province, but the caliph watches his kinsmen, and a suspected rival can be imprisoned or left to die.
tiers.kid: Families descended from the Prophet Muhammad’s clan were the most honoured in the empire.
tiers.rise: Hashimite rank came only by birth in the male line. A prince could rise to the caliphate, or end in prison or worse at the hands of a rival.
tiers.why: Descent from the Banu Hashim, the clan of the Prophet Muhammad, became the highest mark of nobility among Muslims.

tiers.name: Viziers and secretaries
tiers.you: You keep the accounts of the land tax in a government office, as your father did; if your faction wins the vizierate you grow rich, and if it falls you may be fined and tortured for your fortune.
tiers.kid: Viziers and secretaries ran the caliph’s government, kept its accounts and wrote its letters.
tiers.rise: Secretaries rose by skill, family and patronage; many were converts or their sons, and Christians served as secretaries too. A caliph could raise a secretary to the vizierate and ruin him as quickly.
tiers.why: The caliph’s government was run from offices (diwans) for taxes, the army, correspondence and the post.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You were bought as a boy beyond the frontier, trained as a mounted archer and paid a salary in your regiment’s quarter at Samarra, and your commanders make and unmake caliphs.
tiers.kid: Many of the caliph’s soldiers were Turks from Central Asia who fought on horseback with bows.
tiers.rise: A slave boy bought on the steppe could become a general: Itakh began as a cook, and Mu’nis, a Greek eunuch slave, commanded the whole army from 908 to 933. Commanders who lost a struggle at court were dismissed, imprisoned or killed.
tiers.why: The army that won the revolution of 747–750 came from Khurasan, and its men and their sons, the abna al-dawla (“sons of the dynasty”), settled in Baghdad as the regime’s privileged soldiers, paid by the state.

tiers.name: Scholars of religious law
tiers.you: You have studied the Qur’an, the Prophet’s traditions and the law with renowned teachers and may sit as a judge, though the caliph can dismiss you or, as in the Mihna, try to dictate your beliefs.
tiers.kid: The ulama were Muslim scholars who studied the Qur’an and religious law, and some were judges.
tiers.rise: Learning was open to any Muslim who could find teachers, converts and their sons included; a qadi, though, held office only at the caliph’s pleasure.
tiers.why: The ulama were the scholars of the Qur’an, the traditions of the Prophet (hadith) and religious law.

tiers.name: Merchants and bankers
tiers.you: You ship Chinese porcelain and spices through Basra or lend money to the government, and you may grow very rich, though a shipwreck or a greedy soldier could take it all.
tiers.kid: Abbasid merchants sailed as far as China and brought back silk and fine pottery.
tiers.rise: Trade was open to any free man with capital, Muslim or not, and a great financier could win the ear of viziers; but a lost ship or an extortion could ruin a house.
tiers.why: Trade carried honour in a faith whose Prophet had been a merchant, and the caliphate joined the trade of the Indian Ocean, the Mediterranean and the Silk Road.

tiers.name: Muslim townspeople
tiers.you: You work at a trade in the markets of Baghdad and pay the alms tax as a Muslim, and whether your grandfather was an Arab or a Persian convert matters less than it once did.
tiers.kid: Many townspeople were craftsmen and shopkeepers who worked in busy markets.
tiers.rise: Converts joined this rank freely, since conversion lifted the poll tax, and a townsman could rise by trade, by learning or by service in the army or a government office.
tiers.why: The free Muslims of the towns, craftsmen, shopkeepers, porters, water-carriers and labourers, filled the markets of Baghdad, Basra, Kufa and the provincial capitals; Baghdad, founded in 762, was probably the largest…

tiers.name: Protected non-Muslims
tiers.you: You are a Christian, a Jew or a Zoroastrian: you keep your faith and your community’s courts and pay a yearly poll tax, a caliph may order you to wear distinguishing clothes, and you may still serve him as a physician or a secretary.
tiers.kid: Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians kept their own religions but paid a special tax.
tiers.rise: Conversion to Islam lifted the poll tax and opened every career, and conversion spread steadily: Richard Bulliet estimated that Muslims in Iran grew from about 40 per cent of the people in the mid-9th century to nearly 80 per cent by the end of the 11th.
tiers.why: Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians were dhimmis, protected peoples.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You farm a plot in the irrigated plain of Iraq for a landlord who lives in the city, hand over up to half your harvest as land tax, whatever your faith, and may abandon your fields if the tax collectors press too hard.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers who grew wheat, barley and dates and paid heavy taxes on their harvests.
tiers.rise: A peasant who converted escaped the poll tax but not the land tax. Many fled to the towns; others revolted, like the Christian Copts of the Nile Delta in 831–832, after which many of their women and children were sold as slaves.
tiers.why: Most people lived by farming, in the irrigated plain of southern Iraq, the Sawad, in the Nile valley, Iran and Syria, Muslims and non-Muslims alike.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were captured or bought beyond the frontier and now serve in a Baghdad household; your owner may free you as a pious act, and if you are a woman who bears him a child he acknowledges, you cannot be sold and will go free at his death.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; some were later freed.
tiers.rise: Freeing a slave was counted a pious act, and a slave could also buy freedom by contract. Freed slaves became clients (mawali) of their former owners, and many rose high: the mothers of most caliphs had been slaves.
tiers.why: Islamic law forbade enslaving Muslims or protected dhimmis, so slaves came from beyond the frontiers: war captives from Byzantium, Turks from the Central Asian steppe, Slavs and other Europeans brought down the Volga…
